patient.chief_complaint: Witnessed brief shaking then prolonged confusion and abnormal movements for 50 minutes, fever present
patient.hpi: A 66-year-old Hispanic male retired mechanic was brought to the emergency department by his son, who witnessed a brief tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. The patient has no known history of epilepsy. His son reports that over the past 2 weeks, his father had been having progressive memory difficulty, confusion, and behavioral changes — he kept repeating questions, got lost driving to a familiar gas station, and had been sleeping 14-16 hours per day. He had also complained of intermittent headaches. No fever at home was noted initially. After the brief shaking stopped, the patient did not return to baseline. Instead, over the following 20 minutes, the son noticed his father making repetitive unusual hand and finger movements — rubbing his thumb and index finger together continuously — and intermittently smacking his lips. EMS temperature was 38.2°C. He has a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia but no neurological conditions. He takes metformin and lisinopril. Recently, his primary care physician started him on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for a urinary tract infection 12 days ago. He also takes over-the-counter cetirizine for seasonal allergies. No known immunosuppression. Son denies alcohol use, illicit drugs, or recent travel outside the state. No sick contacts. No known tuberculosis exposure. Family history: father had Alzheimer's dementia at 78. Wife died of breast cancer. Son and daughter healthy.

interactions.description: Acyclovir is renally cleared; high-dose IV acyclovir + TMP-SMX can both reduce GFR through tubular competitive inhibition, increasing nephrotoxicity risk
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Discontinue TMP-SMX (UTI should be treated separately with alternative antibiotic if still needed). Monitor creatinine and BUN daily during IV acyclovir. Hold metformin while on IV acyclovir due to nephrotoxicity risk.

interactions.description: TMP-SMX falsely elevates serum creatinine (blocks tubular creatinine secretion) — true GFR may be higher than creatinine-based estimates suggest
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Consider cystatin C for true GFR estimation while TMP-SMX is being discontinued

output.summary: Stop TMP-SMX to reduce nephrotoxicity risk with IV acyclovir. Monitor renal function daily. Hold metformin to prevent lactic acidosis in setting of renal stress.

results.title: Herpes simplex encephalitis: diagnosis and treatment update
results.key_finding: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h for 21 days is standard treatment for HSV-1 encephalitis. Despite treatment, 30-40% of patients have significant neurological sequelae (memory impairment, personality change, epilepsy). NCSE complicating HSV encephalitis requires both antiviral and AED treatment. Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces edema but remains controversial.

output.summary: HSV-1 encephalitis: 21-day acyclovir course mandatory. NCSE is treated with AEDs alongside antivirals. Memory impairment and chronic epilepsy are expected sequelae. Ensure adequate hydration with IV acyclovir to prevent crystallization nephropathy.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Herpes simplex encephalitis type 1 (HSV-1) with non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) from right temporal lobe involvement

differential.key_features: Subacute behavioral decline + NCSE + limbic MRI changes overlap; however HSV PCR positive 10,400 copies/mL is definitive; autoimmune antibodies negative
Age 66 male with subacute decline warrants paraneoplastic consideration; HSV PCR positive is definitive diagnosis; paraneoplastic panel would be sent as secondary workup
CSF shows lymphocytic predominance (not neutrophilic); gram stain/culture negative; procalcitonin only mildly elevated; clinical picture supports viral encephalitis
No prior stroke history; MRI shows active encephalitic changes not chronic infarct; fever and CSF pleocytosis indicate acute infection

critical_actions: Empiric acyclovir IMMEDIATELY — fatal delay if HSV diagnosis missed
LP with HSV PCR — definitive diagnostic test
MRI brain with FLAIR + DWI — classic right temporal HSV-1 pattern
Stop TMP-SMX — nephrotoxicity with IV acyclovir; hold metformin
21-day acyclovir course — do NOT stop early when patient improves
contraindicated_actions: Delaying acyclovir pending MRI or LP results — HSV encephalitis is fatal without early treatment
Stopping acyclovir prematurely (before 21 days) — relapses are common; must complete full course
Continuing TMP-SMX with IV acyclovir — combined nephrotoxicity; also TMP elevates creatinine artifactually
key_reasoning_points: HSV-1 encephalitis classically affects temporal and frontal limbic structures — right or bilateral temporal FLAIR changes + behavioral symptoms + fever
NCSE complicating HSV encephalitis arises from acute temporal lobe destruction — treat both the infection (acyclovir) and the seizures (AED)
Empiric acyclovir should never wait for CSF results — mortality increases dramatically with every hour of delay
TMP-SMX falsely elevates creatinine and competes with acyclovir for tubular secretion — stop TMP-SMX during acyclovir therapy
Resident-level challenge: distinguish HSV encephalitis from autoimmune limbic encephalitis; both show temporal FLAIR changes; CSF HSV PCR is definitive

metadata.teaching_points: HSV-1 encephalitis causing NCSE; empiric acyclovir before test results; TMP-SMX nephrotoxicity with acyclovir; 21-day course; temporal FLAIR on MRI
metadata.pitfalls: Delaying acyclovir for diagnostic workup; stopping TMP-SMX late; attributing NCSE to metabolic without considering HSV
metadata.clinical_pearl: Subacute behavioral decline + fever + temporal FLAIR + NCSE in elderly man = HSV encephalitis first. Start acyclovir FIRST. CSF HSV PCR confirms.
